title: differential-pad-gain-scheduler
author: Jared Kim
description:
Motivation: Reduce padding waste while preserving latency SLOs by making scheduling decisions that explicitly trade expected pad savings against induced queuing delay. This PR introduces the 'Differential Pad Gain Scheduler' (DPGS), a scheduler that computes per-slot expected pad reduction (pad gain) and uses a tunable cost function combining kernel execution cost, KV-cache hit probability delta, and added wait time to decide whether to coalesce sequences or dispatch early.

What changed (summary): Implemented a pad-gain estimator, integrated it into the runtime request coagulation path, added a scheduling policy that uses a harmonic-weighted objective (latency vs. token-cost) and per-model kernel cost curves, and extended the continuous-batcher to expose candidate merge scores for observability/ablation. Also added unit and benchmark tests and a small canary rollout script for Dedicated pools.

Checklist:
- [x] Pad gain estimator and unit tests
- [x] Scheduler policy with tunable knobs (pad_gain_threshold, latency_penalty_weight)
- [x] Kernel cost curve integration for model families (llama, redwood-small, redwood-large)
- [x] KV cache delta model (empirical fallback for warm cache metrics)
- [x] Integration tests and end-to-end bench harness
- [x] Console metrics + rollout gating flags

Design notes (single paragraph): Unlike pure bucketing or greedy length coalescers, DPGS computes an expected token savings (pad gain) for each potential merge and normalizes that against the marginal latency impact using recent slot wait-time statistics. We use a small lookback window (configurable, default 1s) to estimate the probability that a slot will fill naturally; pad gain is discounted by the probability of a natural fill. Kernel-specific cost curves (precomputed offline and loaded at runtime) allow the scheduler to prefer merges that are kernel-friendly (e.g., merges that increase sequence length into an efficient kernel shape). The system also accounts for KV-cache delta: merging a short prompt with a long context may reduce cache reuse — this delta is estimated from recent rolling counters and a small Bayesian prior for cold starts.

Benchmarks (summary): micro-bench on Dedicated-rt1 (A100-equivalent) using production prompt mix: token-cost reduction 9.8% (median), P95 token latency change +1.6ms (within SLO), KV-cache hit rate improved +3.2% for long-session workloads, contextual throughput +6.5% under 1s load. Tail latency regression guarded by latency_penalty_weight; default config picked to keep P95 within 2ms of baseline while maximizing pad savings.

Rollout plan: feature flag gated; start with 10% of traffic on low-priority Dedicated pools, monitor cost-per-token and P95 latency on route dashboards, promote to 50% if no regressions for 24 hours. Canary script included at tooling/canary/dpgs_canary.sh.

Risks and mitigations: Incorrect KV delta estimation can cause regressions for highly stateful sessions — mitigated by conservative prior and immediate auto-fallback to greedy dispatch if bucket miss rate increases. Large models with non-monotonic kernel cost curves are handled by model-specific curves; if a curve is missing, DPGS falls back to a length-bucketer with existing defaults.

release_notes: Introduce Differential Pad Gain Scheduler: A runtime policy that balances expected padding savings against latency impact and KV-cache delta. Opt-in via feature flag 'dpgs'. Default hidden behind rollout gating. Expect ~8-10% token-cost savings on mixed production prompt mixes with minimal tail latency impact.
notes_for_oncall: If increased P95 is observed after rollout, flip deploy/feature flag dpgs->off; watch KV cache miss counters (runtime.kv.delta_miss_rate) and pad_gain_reject_rate metric. Canary script can revert within 5 minutes.
